data.text/markdown:
Classification in 2D: How Neural Networks Learn Features

Imagine you are given a map covered in colored dots, and your job is to teach a computer to guess the color of any new dot just from its position. This is called classification. The catch: in this example, the colors are arranged so that no straight line can split them apart. Simple methods that draw straight dividing lines will fail. In this notebook you will see how a neural network solves the problem. Instead of drawing curvy lines directly, it learns to re-draw the map: it moves the dots to new positions where the colors can be split with straight lines. These new positions are called features, and learning good features is the key idea behind modern AI. We will go step by step:
  1. Create a dataset that is hard to classify.
  2. Build a small neural network.
  3. Train it and check how well it does.
  4. Peek inside the network to see the features it learned.

Step 1: The data

Each dot below is one data point. It is described by just two numbers, its horizontal and vertical position (Feature 1 and Feature 2). Its color is the class (the answer we want the computer to predict):
  • Class 0 and Class 1: two interlocking half-moons in the middle.
  • Class 2: a ring that surrounds both moons.
Use the slider to change how many points are generated for each class.

Many classic methods (for example, logistic regression) can only draw straight boundaries between classes. They work well when the groups sit in different regions of the map, but here any straight line would cut through at least one moon or through the ring. We could hand-design new measurements to help, such as "distance from the center", which would pick out the ring. But that requires a human to understand the data first. A neural network discovers useful measurements like this on its own.

data.text/markdown:
Holding back an "exam"

Before training, we set aside 20% of the points as a test set. The network never sees these points while learning. Afterwards we use them as an exam to check that it truly learned the pattern, rather than just memorizing the points it was shown (the training set).
Training points: 480    Test points: 120

data.text/html:
Step 2: The neural network

A neural network is built from layers of simple units called neurons. Each neuron combines the numbers it receives into a single new number, a bit like a tiny detector that responds to a particular pattern. Stacking layers lets the network build complex patterns out of simple ones. Our network passes each point through these layers:
Layer Size What it does
Input 2 The point's position (Feature 1, Feature 2)
Hidden layer 1 16 neurons Detects simple patterns in the position
Hidden layer 2 16 neurons Combines those into more complex patterns
Hidden layer 3 2 neurons The learned features, squeezed down to 2 numbers
Output 3 One score per class; the highest score is the prediction
After each hidden layer there is a ReLU step, which keeps positive values and turns negative values into zero. This simple "on/off" behavior is what lets the network bend and fold the map instead of only stretching it. Notice the deliberate bottleneck: the last hidden layer has only 2 neurons. That means every point is turned into just two new numbers, which we can plot later to see exactly how the network has re-drawn the map.
The printout below lists the layers in order:
  • Linear(in_features=2, out_features=16) is a layer of 16 neurons, each taking a weighted sum of the 2 inputs. The weights are the knobs the network adjusts while learning.
  • ReLU() is the "keep positives, zero out negatives" step.
  • The final Linear(in_features=2, out_features=3) turns the 2 learned features into 3 class scores.

data.text/markdown:
Step 3: Training

At first the network's weights are random, so its guesses are random too. Training repeats a simple loop:
  1. Guess the class of a small batch of training points.
  2. Measure how wrong the guesses were. This error score is called the loss.
  3. Nudge every weight slightly in the direction that would have reduced the loss.
One full pass through all the training points is called an epoch. We train for 20 epochs. Note: the network is trained once (20 epochs) when the notebook opens. Pressing Train Model continues training the same network from where it left off. Pressing Reset Model throws away everything learned and trains a fresh network, starting from a new set of random weights.

Reading the results

The learning curve shows the loss after each epoch. A curve that drops and then flattens out means the network is learning and gradually settling on a good solution. If it stays high, the network got stuck; try pressing Train Model again, or Reset Model to start over from new random weights. The scores underneath are measured on the test set, the "exam" points the network never saw during training.
  • Accuracy: the fraction of test points that were given the correct class.
  • Precision: when the network says "this is class X", how often is it right? (averaged over the three classes)
  • Recall: of all the points that truly are class X, how many did the network find? (averaged over the three classes)
With balanced classes like ours, all three numbers are usually close to each other.

data.text/markdown:
Step 4: Looking inside the black box

Now for the most interesting part. Remember the 2-neuron bottleneck layer? For every point in the dataset we record the two numbers that come out of that layer and plot them, keeping each point's original color. This shows the data through the eyes of the network: it is the re-drawn map that the final layer uses to make its decision.

data.text/html:
A few things you may notice:
  • Many points sit exactly on an axis or at the corner (0, 0). This is the ReLU step at work: any negative value is set to zero.
  • The picture looks different each time you press Reset Model and retrain. There are many ways to re-draw the map, and the random starting weights decide which one the network finds. Sometimes it lands on a poor one where the colors still overlap; if so, reset and try again.

data.text/markdown:
Summary

  • Some problems cannot be solved with straight lines in their original form.
  • Hidden layers transform the data, moving points into a new space (the learned features).
  • In that new space, the final layer only needs to draw straight lines. Neural networks learn the features and the classifier together, directly from examples.

Things to try

  • Press Train Model several times and watch how the learning curve and the hidden-layer plot change.
  • Press Reset Model a few times and compare the hidden-layer plots that different random starting points produce.
  • Move the Samples per class slider to use more or fewer points, then retrain. Does less data make learning harder?
  • Compare the hidden-layer plot from a poorly trained network (high loss) with a well trained one.
